items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: London to Tokyo flights cross Siberia — not because Russia is convenient
items.claim: On a flat map, the shortest path between London and Tokyo looks like a horizontal line through Central Asia. The ACTUAL shortest path on Earth's surface arcs north over Siberia. That's the great-circle route.
items.prompt: Why is the great-circle route shortest?

options.text: Any geodesic (shortest path) on a sphere is part of a great circle — a circle whose plane passes through the sphere's centre. Latitude lines (except the equator) are NOT great circles, so flying along a latitude isn't optimal

items.reveal:
A geodesic is the shortest path between two points on a surface. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are arcs of great circles — circles whose centre coincides with the sphere's centre.

All meridians (longitude lines, including the prime meridian and date line) are great circles. The equator is a great circle. Lines of latitude EXCEPT the equator are NOT great circles — they're small circles whose plane does not pass through Earth's centre.

London-Tokyo: separated by ~9600 km along the great-circle route, ~12000 km if you fly along the line of latitude (~50°N).

Map projections distort geodesics:
- Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569): preserves angles (conformal), shows rhumb lines as straight, but distorts areas and great-circle paths.
- Gnomonic projection: shows great circles as straight lines, but is unsuitable as a navigational chart.
- Robinson, Mollweide: balance distortions in different ways.

Airlines plan routes along great circles, adjusted for winds (jetstream eastbound from US to Europe saves an hour). 'Polar' routes from North America to East Asia routinely cross the Arctic.

In general relativity, geodesics on curved spacetime trace the paths of free-falling objects — gravity IS geodesic motion through curved spacetime.
items.why: Maps lie about distances. Modern navigation requires understanding that the shortest path on a sphere is curved on a flat map. The intuition fails everywhere except locally.

items.title: A bottle with no inside
items.claim: A normal bottle has an inside and an outside, separated by the bottle wall. The Klein bottle has no inside. There is only one surface — what looks like 'inside' is connected to 'outside' through the surface itself.
items.prompt: How is the Klein bottle different from a regular surface?

options.text: It's non-orientable — there is no consistent way to assign 'outward normals'; a left-handed walker traversing it can come back as right-handed
It's actually two surfaces glued together
Klein bottles only exist in imagination

items.reveal:
Klein constructed the bottle as a 2D analogue of the Möbius strip — but closed. To build one in 3D, you must let the bottle 'pass through itself' (a fake self-intersection). Properly, it lives in 4-dimensional space, where it has no intersection.

In rigorous terms: the Klein bottle is a non-orientable, closed 2-manifold with Euler characteristic 0. It cannot be embedded in 3D Euclidean space without self-intersection.

The Möbius strip (Möbius, 1858) is a 2D example with boundary: cut one open and you get a long strip; cut it in half lengthwise and you get a single longer Möbius strip, not two.

Non-orientable surfaces matter in physics (some condensed matter systems behave like Möbius strips), engineering (conveyor belt design uses Möbius topology to wear evenly), and cosmology (toy models of non-orientable universes have been considered, though our universe seems to be orientable).
items.why: 3D objects have an obvious inside and outside. Topology shows some 2D surfaces don't — the apparently obvious 'inside/outside' distinction is a special feature of orientable manifolds.
